about: Repair batch 5 (2026-10-25): the 76 held-back questions whose automatic confidence was 0.70-0.75 (the bank was ranked with --threshold 0.75). Their low scores came mostly from the structural signals (support 0.67, grounding 0.5: two near-duplicate points from one slide line), not from wrong facts, so each was read by hand. Same rule as batches 1-4: short points, one claim each, naming the mechanism, no lists of examples, the reference answer states every point, no point asks for more than the question. 63 activated after fixes (34 most-asked topics first), including real errors: self join called 'a special case of cross join', full outer join via UNION said to 'introduce duplicates', circuit switching said to 'save' and packet switching to 'waste' bandwidth, M:N explained as 'multiple parents', FCFS given a time slice, 'the definitions provided' (unseen text), a scenario naming classes the candidate never saw, and questions whose points missed half of what they ask (RAID 5, adjacency-matrix space, readers-writers starvation, Object class). 13 kept held back with a score and note: open-ended or one-of-many-answers questions, near-duplicates of served questions, slide-phrase trivia and one false premise (the List interface does not make insertion efficient). Point-quote links below 0.35 that remain are genuine but terse slide lines (a formula, a code line, 'Cbest(n) = 1', a one-line starvation remark): BCNF medium2 KP0, best/worst KP0, double hashing KP1, DIP KP1, readers-writers KP2, DFS paths KP2. Also sharpened after a cross-question check: dsa.insertion_sort.hard2 (a selection-sort answer matched it), ooad.design_pattern_categories.hard2 and ooad.classes_and_objects.medium1 (a constructor answer matched generic points). slide_rag/rank_bank.py now keeps the active flag of hand-reviewed questions, so re-ranking cannot undo this batch.

cn.dhcp.hard2.quality_note: points were about leases in general, not renewal; question reworded to match; not hard (repair 5)
cn.dhcp.hard2.question: Why does DHCP give out IP addresses as time-limited leases instead of permanently, and why does this suit mobile users?
cn.dhcp.hard2.reference_answer: A DHCP server lends each host an IP address for a limited lease time, and the host must renew the lease to keep the address. A host only holds its address while it is connected, so when it leaves or stops renewing, the address goes back to the pool and can be reused by another host. This lets a network serve more hosts over time than it has addresses. It also supports mobile users who join and leave networks often: they get an address automatically when they arrive and give it back when they leave, without manual configuration.

key_points.point: A host holds its address only while connected, so the address can be reused afterwards.
Leases support mobile users who join and leave the network.
key_points.followup_answer: It gets an address automatically when it joins and gives it back when it leaves, with no manual setup.

key_points.point: A MAC address is a 48-bit hardware address burned into the network card.
It is used to deliver frames between interfaces on the same local network.

cn.mac_addressing.easy1.reference_answer: A MAC address is a 48-bit hardware address burned into the network card (the NIC's ROM) by the manufacturer, written like 1A-2F-BB-76-09-AD, and unique to that card. It works at the data link layer: it is used locally to deliver a frame from one interface to another interface on the same local network (subnet). To reach a host on another network, IP addresses are used, and ARP finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address on the local network.

cn.nat.easy1.quality_note: narrow security question widened to what NAT is; address-change point moved to the reference (repair 5)
cn.nat.easy1.question: Explain what NAT is and how it helps protect a local network.
cn.nat.easy1.reference_answer: NAT (network address translation) lets all the devices of a local network share one public IP address: the NAT router replaces the private source address of each outgoing packet with its public address and translates replies back. Just one IP address is needed from the ISP for all devices. Because the outside world only sees the router's address, devices inside the local network are not directly addressable or visible from outside, which protects them from unsolicited connections. Internal addresses can also be changed without telling the outside world.

key_points.point: Devices inside are not directly reachable from the outside world.
All devices share one public IP address that the router translates.
key_points.quote: just one IP address needed from provider ISP for all devices
key_points.followup: How does the router know which inside device a reply belongs to?
key_points.followup_answer: It keeps a NAT translation table mapping each (private address, port) to the (public address, new port) it used.

cn.packet_switching_vs_circuit_switching.quality_note: reference had bandwidth backwards (circuit 'saves', packet 'wastes'); garbled quote replaced (repair 5)
cn.packet_switching_vs_circuit_switching.reference_answer: Circuit switching reserves a fixed amount of bandwidth for each connection for its whole duration; these dedicated resources are not shared, so the reserved bandwidth sits idle whenever the user is silent. Packet switching does not reserve anything: link bandwidth is shared on demand among all users, which uses it more efficiently for bursty traffic but means packets can queue. In circuit switching all data follows the same path, so messages arrive in order; in packet switching packets may take different paths and arrive out of order, so they are reassembled at the destination.

key_points.point: Circuit switching reserves fixed bandwidth for each connection; packet switching shares it on demand.
key_points.quote: Q: human analogies of reserved resources (circuit switching) versus
key_points.followup_answer: Each user's reserved bandwidth stays allocated even when that user is idle, so it is wasted.

key_points.point: In packet switching, packets may arrive out of order and are reassembled at the destination.

cn.tcp_congestion_control.easy1.quality_note: points shortened; reference states the ACK point (repair 5)
cn.tcp_congestion_control.easy1.reference_answer: TCP congestion control lets each sender adjust its sending rate to what the network can carry, using its own feedback. Each ACK for new data shows the network is delivering segments, so the sender increases its rate as ACKs arrive. A lost segment is taken as a sign of congestion, so the sender cuts its rate. By probing upward until loss and backing off after it, senders avoid overloading routers, which prevents congestion collapse, where the network is so overloaded that almost nothing useful gets through.

key_points.point: The sender cuts its rate when a segment is lost.
The sender increases its rate as ACKs arrive.

dbms.boyce_codd_normal_form_bcnf.easy1.reference_answer: A relation schema R is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form if, for every non-trivial dependency X -> A that holds in R, X is a superkey of R. In other words, only a key can determine other attributes. BCNF is stricter than 3NF: every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but 3NF also allows X -> A when A is a prime attribute. BCNF removes the redundancy and update anomalies caused by dependencies on non-keys.

key_points.point: In BCNF, for every non-trivial dependency X -> A, X is a superkey.
BCNF is stricter than 3NF.
It has a dependency X -> A where X is not a superkey and A is a prime attribute.
BCNF requires X to be a superkey for every dependency X -> A.

dbms.concurrency_anomalies.medium2.quality_note: points split into the cause and the effect (repair 5); effect point made specific after a cross-question check

key_points.point: Another transaction changes the item between T's two reads of it.
So T's second read of the item returns a different value from its first read.

dbms.concurrency_anomalies.medium2.reference_answer: An unrepeatable read happens when a transaction T reads the same item twice and another transaction T' changes the item between the two reads. So T's second read of the item returns a different value from its first read, even though T itself changed nothing. If T makes decisions from the first value, for example checking a balance and then using it, its logic becomes wrong. It is a concurrency anomaly because it only happens when transactions interleave: run serially, T would see the same value both times. Isolation levels from REPEATABLE READ up prevent it.

dbms.foreign_key.easy1.quality_note: ALTER TABLE trivia point replaced by the referential-integrity rule (repair 5)
dbms.foreign_key.easy1.reference_answer: A foreign key is a column, or set of columns, in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It enforces referential integrity: every foreign-key value must already exist as a primary-key value in the referenced table, or be NULL. The DBMS rejects inserts or updates that would break this, and deleting a referenced row is rejected or propagated (for example with ON DELETE CASCADE). This prevents orphan rows that point to nothing.

key_points.point: A foreign key is a column that refers to the primary key of another table.
Each foreign-key value must exist as a primary key in the other table, or be NULL.
key_points.quote: Referential integrity constraints : The “foreign key “ must have a value that is already present as a primary key, or may be null
key_points.followup: What can happen when you delete a row that other rows refer to?
key_points.followup_answer: The delete is rejected, or, if a referential action such as ON DELETE CASCADE is set, it propagates to the referring rows.

key_points.point: An inner join keeps only pairs of rows that satisfy the join condition.
Each matching pair is combined into one result row.
READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads.
REPEATABLE READ prevents both dirty and non-repeatable reads.
READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads.
key_points.quote: READ COMMITTED: Only reads data that has been committed.
key_points.followup: What problem can still happen under REPEATABLE READ?
key_points.followup_answer: Phantom rows: a repeated query can return new rows that another transaction inserted.

dbms.outer_joins.hard2.quality_note: reference said UNION 'may introduce duplicates' (it removes them; UNION ALL repeats matched rows); question reworded (repair 5)
dbms.outer_joins.hard2.question: MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN. How can you get the same result, and what do you have to be careful about?
dbms.outer_joins.hard2.reference_answer: Run a LEFT OUTER JOIN and a RIGHT OUTER JOIN of the two tables and combine them with UNION. The left join gives every row of the first table, the right join every row of the second, and unmatched rows are padded with NULLs for the other table's columns. Matched rows appear in both halves, so UNION is used because it removes those duplicates; UNION ALL would list every matched row twice. The catch is that UNION also removes rows that are genuinely identical in the data, so the result can differ from a true FULL OUTER JOIN if the tables contain duplicate rows.

key_points.point: Combine a LEFT and a RIGHT outer join with UNION.
key_points.followup_answer: UNION removes the matched rows that both joins return; UNION ALL would show them twice.

key_points.point: Unmatched rows are padded with NULLs for the other table's columns.

dbms.self_join_and_cross_join.easy1.quality_note: reference called a self join a special cross join with no condition (wrong) and the points covered only cross join; question narrowed to cross join (repair 5)
dbms.self_join_and_cross_join.easy1.question: Explain what a cross join is and how many rows it returns.
dbms.self_join_and_cross_join.easy1.reference_answer: A cross join returns the Cartesian product of two tables: every row of the first table is combined with every row of the second. It does not use a join condition, so it does not match columns at all. If the tables have m and n rows, the result has m x n rows, for example 8 x 7 = 56. A WHERE clause can filter the result afterwards, which turns it into an ordinary inner join.

key_points.point: A cross join returns the Cartesian product: every row paired with every row.
key_points.followup_answer: 56 rows: 8 x 7.

key_points.point: It uses no join condition.

dsa.best_worst_and_average_case.medium1.quality_note: garbled quotes replaced; worst-case point added (repair 5)
dsa.best_worst_and_average_case.medium1.reference_answer: For sequential search, the best case is when the key is in the first position, so only one comparison is needed: Cbest(n) = 1. The worst case is when the key is in the last position or not in the list at all, so all n elements are compared: Cworst(n) = n. The average case is not (best + worst) / 2: it is the expected number of comparisons over all inputs, weighted by how likely each input is. For example, if the search succeeds with probability p and every position is equally likely, Cavg(n) = p(n + 1)/2 + n(1 - p).

key_points.point: Best case: the key is in the first position, so one comparison.
key_points.quote: Best-Case: Cbest(n) = 1

key_points.point: The average case weighs every input by its probability; it is not the mean of best and worst.
key_points.quote: Average case: The algorithm runs the fastest among all possible inputs of size n. How to find the average case efficiency? NOT the average of worst and best case

key_points.point: Worst case: the key is last or absent, so n comparisons.
key_points.quote: Worst-Case: Cworst(n) = n
key_points.followup: Which inputs give the worst case for sequential search?
key_points.followup_answer: A key in the last position, or a key that is not in the list at all.

dsa.graph_representation.easy1.quality_note: adjacency-matrix space was missing from the points (repair 5)
dsa.graph_representation.easy1.reference_answer: An adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices is a V x V table, so it always needs O(V^2) space, whatever the number of edges. An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, only the edges that actually exist, so it needs O(V + E) space. For a sparse graph with few edges most matrix entries are zeros, so the adjacency list uses far less space; for a dense graph the two are similar, and the matrix gives O(1) edge lookup.

key_points.point: An adjacency list needs O(V + E) space.
An adjacency list is better for sparse graphs.
An adjacency matrix always needs O(V^2) space.
key_points.quote: space complexity is O(v2). v2 locations are required for graph with v nodes
key_points.followup: When would you still choose an adjacency matrix?
key_points.followup_answer: For dense graphs, or when you need to check whether an edge exists in O(1) time.

dsa.graph_representation.medium2.quality_note: thin: two points said the same thing; second point now the missing-edge value (repair 5)
dsa.graph_representation.medium2.reference_answer: For a weighted graph, entry [i][j] of the adjacency matrix stores the weight (cost or distance) of the edge from vertex i to vertex j instead of just 1. Pairs with no edge need a special value that cannot be a real weight, usually infinity (or 0 if zero-weight edges are impossible). For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric. Looking up any edge's weight takes O(1) time.

key_points.point: Entry [i][j] stores the weight of the edge from i to j.
Pairs of nodes with no edge store a special value such as infinity instead of a cost.

key_points.point: Double hashing uses a second hash function to choose the probe step after a collision.
key_points.followup_answer: The probe would never move, so the second hash function must never return 0.

key_points.point: Different keys get different probe steps, which avoids the clustering of linear probing.
key_points.quote: hash(key) = (hash1(key) + i * hash2(key)) % tableSize

dsa.hash_functions.medium1.reference_answer: Double hashing is an open-addressing method that uses a second hash function to choose the probe step after a collision: the i-th probe is (hash1(key) + i * hash2(key)) % tableSize. Different keys get different probe steps, which avoids the clustering of linear probing. With linear probing every colliding key steps by 1, so occupied slots form long runs that keep growing and slow down searches and inserts. The second hash function must never return 0, and the table size is usually prime so the probe sequence can reach every slot.

ooad.classes_and_objects.medium1.reference_answer: A class is a blueprint: it declares the attributes and methods that its objects will have, but it is only a description. Objects are created from it with new, and each object is an instance of the class. Each object has its own values for the class's attributes (its own state) and shares the behaviour defined by the methods. Every Java class implicitly inherits from Object, the root of the class hierarchy, so every object has common methods such as toString(), equals() and hashCode(), and any object can be referred to by a variable of type Object.

ooad.dependency_inversion_principle.hard.question: An OrderService class saves orders through a Database interface. What goes wrong if it used a concrete MongoDBDatabase class directly instead, and how does this relate to the Dependency Inversion Principle?

key_points.point: High-level and low-level modules should both depend on abstractions.
Depending on the abstraction instead of the concrete class lets the database be swapped without changing OrderService.

ooad.dependency_inversion_principle.hard.reference_answer: If OrderService used MongoDBDatabase directly, the high-level business class would depend on a low-level concrete class: they would be tightly coupled, and switching to another database, or testing OrderService with a fake one, would mean changing OrderService. The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level and low-level modules should both depend on abstractions. Depending on the abstraction instead of the concrete class lets the database be swapped without changing OrderService: MongoDBDatabase and MySQLDatabase both implement the Database interface, and the right one is passed in.

os.fragmentation.easy1.quality_note: duplicate point replaced by the cause (fixed-size blocks) (repair 5)
os.fragmentation.easy1.reference_answer: Internal fragmentation is memory that is allocated to a process but not used by it: the allocated block is slightly larger than the request, and the difference is wasted inside the partition. It happens because memory is handed out in fixed-size units, such as fixed partitions or page frames, so a request is rounded up to a whole unit. For example, with 4 KB pages, a 9 KB process needs three pages and wastes 3 KB in the last one.

key_points.point: Internal fragmentation is allocated memory that the process does not use.
It happens because memory is given out in fixed-size blocks.
key_points.quote: Divide physical memory into fixed-sized blocks called frames
key_points.followup: How is it different from external fragmentation?
key_points.followup_answer: External fragmentation is free memory between allocations that is enough in total but not contiguous.

os.round_robin_scheduling.easy1.quality_note: time quantum point added; follow-up said FCFS has a time slice (repair 5)
os.round_robin_scheduling.easy1.reference_answer: Round-robin scheduling is designed for time-sharing systems. It is like FCFS, but with preemption: each process in the ready queue gets the CPU for at most one time quantum (typically 10-100 ms). If it has not finished when the quantum ends, it is preempted and put at the back of the ready queue. FCFS instead lets a process run until it finishes or blocks, so a long job can make short ones wait; round robin gives every process a regular turn and better response time.

key_points.point: Each process runs for at most one time quantum, then goes to the back of the queue.
key_points.quote: The CPU scheduler goes around the ready queue, allocating the CPU to each process for a time interval of up to 1 time quantum
key_points.followup: What happens if the time quantum is made very large?
key_points.followup_answer: Round robin behaves like FCFS.

key_points.point: Unlike FCFS, round robin preempts a running process.
key_points.followup_answer: Round robin preempts a process when its time quantum ends; FCFS never interrupts a running process, it runs until it finishes or blocks.

os.thrashing.easy1.quality_note: 'severe performance problems' point replaced by what thrashing is (repair 5)
os.thrashing.easy1.reference_answer: Thrashing is when a process, or the whole system, is busy swapping pages in and out instead of executing. It happens when the total size of the localities of the running processes is larger than physical memory, usually because the degree of multiprogramming is too high: each process keeps faulting on pages that were just evicted. CPU utilization drops, and the OS may then add even more processes, making it worse. It is limited with local replacement or the working-set model.

key_points.point: Thrashing is when a process spends its time swapping pages in and out instead of executing.
key_points.quote: Thrashing ≡ a process is busy swapping pages in and out

key_points.point: It happens when the processes' localities do not fit in memory.

cn.link_state_routing.medium2.reference_answer: In link-state routing, each router measures the cost of its direct links and broadcasts this link-state information to every other router in the network. Since every router receives every other router's link costs, all nodes end up with the same complete view of the topology and link costs. Each router then runs Dijkstra's algorithm on that map itself to compute least-cost paths to all destinations.

key_points.followup: What does each router do with this information?

A foreign-key constraint is added to the new relation schema, so its ID must refer to an existing instructor. dbms.relationships_and_cardinality.hard2.quality_note: reference explained M:N as 'multiple parents'; the real reason is one value per foreign-key cell (repair 5)
dbms.relationships_and_cardinality.hard2.reference_answer: A cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N or M:N) says how many entities each entity can be related to, and it decides where the foreign keys go: for 1:1 or 1:N the key of one side can be stored as a foreign key in the other table (the 'many' side for 1:N). An M:N relationship cannot be stored that way, because a foreign-key column holds one value per row, and each entity on either side may be related to many entities on the other. So a separate relationship table (junction table) is created whose rows hold pairs of keys, one from each side, plus any attributes of the relationship. This turns the M:N relationship into two 1:N relationships.

key_points.point: The cardinality ratio decides which table gets the foreign key.
An M:N relationship needs a separate table holding pairs of keys.
key_points.quote: For each regular binary M:N relationship type R, create a new relation S to represent R. This is a relationship relation.

key_points.point: A cycle in the precedence graph means the schedule is not conflict serializable.
There is an edge Ti -> Tj when an operation of Ti conflicts with a later operation of Tj.
key_points.quote: 4. For each case in S where Tj executes a write_item(X) after Ti executes a write_item(X), create an edge (Ti → Tj) in the precedence graph.

dbms.schedules_and_serializability.mediu.reference_answer: To test conflict serializability, build a precedence graph with one node per transaction. There is an edge Ti -> Tj when an operation of Ti conflicts with a later operation of Tj: both access the same item and at least one of them writes it (Tj reads X after Ti writes X, Tj writes X after Ti reads X, or Tj writes X after Ti writes X). A cycle in the precedence graph means the schedule is not conflict serializable, because the transactions in the cycle would each have to come before the other. If there is no cycle, the schedule is conflict serializable, and a topological order of the graph gives an equivalent serial schedule.

dbms.set_operations_in_sql.easy1.reference_answer: The UNION operator combines the rows returned by two (or more) SELECT statements into a single result and removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps them. Both SELECTs must be union compatible: they must return the same number of columns, and corresponding columns must have compatible types. This lets you merge data from different queries or tables, for example all students and all staff who live in one city, into one list.

dbms.triggers.medium1.reference_answer: A trigger is code the database runs automatically when an event such as an INSERT happens on a table. To validate marks, a BEFORE INSERT trigger checks each new row before it is stored: if the mark is outside 0 to 100, the trigger raises an error, so the insert fails and the bad row is never stored. Because the check runs inside the database, it applies to every application and every insert, which enforces data integrity in one place.

If the value is invalid, the trigger raises an error and the row is not inserted.

dsa.huffman_coding.medium1.reference_answer: Huffman coding builds a binary tree from the symbol frequencies, repeatedly merging the two least frequent trees, and reads each symbol's code from the path from the root to it: 0 for a left branch, 1 for a right branch. Every symbol is a leaf, so no symbol's path passes through another symbol, and therefore no codeword is a prefix of another (a prefix-free code). This matters because the compressed bits can then be decoded unambiguously without separators: reading bits from the root, you reach a leaf exactly at the end of each codeword.

key_points.point: Huffman codes are read from a binary tree in which every symbol is a leaf.
No codeword is a prefix of another, so decoding needs no separators.
Prim's algorithm grows a single tree, adding edges that join new vertices to it.
Kruskal's algorithm grows a forest of trees that are merged.
key_points.quote: Prim's algorithm is very similar to Kruskal's: whereas Kruskal's 'grows' a forest of trees, Prim's algorithm grows a single tree until it becomes the minimum spanning tree.
key_points.followup: Which edge does Prim's algorithm add next?
key_points.followup_answer: The cheapest edge joining a vertex in the tree to a vertex outside it.

dsa.prim_s_algorithm.medium1.reference_answer: Prim's algorithm grows a single tree, adding edges that join new vertices to it: at each step it adds the cheapest edge connecting a vertex in the tree to a vertex outside it. Kruskal's algorithm grows a forest of trees that are merged: it takes edges in increasing order of weight from anywhere in the graph and adds each one that does not form a cycle, so several separate trees exist until they join. This is why Prim's needs only a priority queue of edges leaving the tree, while Kruskal's needs sorting plus Union-Find to detect cycles.

ooad.abstract_classes.medium1.reference_answer: An abstract class supports abstraction by defining what its subclasses have in common while leaving some details to them. Abstract classes cannot be instantiated, which reinforces their role in abstraction: they describe a general concept rather than a concrete thing. They provide a template for common methods that subclasses must implement, and can also contain concrete methods shared by all subclasses, which reduces duplicated code. In an inheritance hierarchy this gives every subclass the same structure while each fills in its own specific behaviour.

ooad.coupling_and_cohesion.medium2.reference_answer: Low coupling means classes depend little on the details of other classes, so a change in one class has little impact on the others; they interact through well-defined interfaces or abstractions. This makes the system easier to maintain and change. It must be balanced with high cohesion: each class should keep closely related, focused responsibilities. Pushing coupling down by merging everything into a few big classes would give low cohesion, and such classes are hard to understand, reuse and maintain. Together, low coupling and high cohesion keep a design flexible and maintainable.

ooad.this_and_super_keywords.hard2.question: What happens if a subclass constructor does not call a superclass constructor explicitly, and when must it call super(...) itself?
ooad.this_and_super_keywords.hard2.reference_answer: Objects are built from the top of the hierarchy down, so a superclass constructor always runs first. If a subclass constructor does not call one explicitly, the compiler inserts super() as its first statement, which calls the superclass's no-argument constructor. If the superclass has no no-argument constructor (for example it only has Shape(int width, int height)), that implicit call fails to compile, so the subclass constructor must call super(...) with the right arguments itself, as its first statement.

key_points.followup_answer: As the first statement of the subclass constructor.

os.file_allocation_methods.medium2.question: What are the disadvantages of indexed allocation compared with linked allocation?
os.file_allocation_methods.medium2.reference_answer: Indexed allocation keeps all of a file's block pointers in an index block, which gives direct access, but it has two costs compared with linked allocation. Its pointer overhead is greater: every file needs at least one whole index block for its pointers, whereas linked allocation only stores one pointer inside each data block. This is especially wasteful for very small files: a file of 2-3 blocks still uses an entire index block just for a few pointers.

key_points.point: Indexed allocation has more pointer overhead than linked allocation.
Very small files still need a whole index block, which wastes space.

os.resource_allocation_graph.easy1.reference_answer: A claim edge Pi -> Rj in a resource-allocation graph shows that process Pi may request resource Rj at some time in the future. It points the same way as a request edge but is drawn as a dashed line. All claim edges must be declared before the process starts, so the system knows each process's possible future requests in advance. When Pi actually requests Rj, the claim edge becomes a request edge, and when the resource is released it goes back to a claim edge. Claim edges are used for deadlock avoidance: a request is granted only if converting it to an assignment edge does not create a cycle.

dsa.graph_connectivity_and_path_finding..reference_answer: The algorithm runs a DFS from the source while keeping the current path in an array. It marks each node as visited when it is added to the path so the path never loops. When the current node is the destination, the whole path is printed. Then it backtracks: it unmarks the node and removes it from the path before returning, so the node can be used again in other paths. Because every branch is tried and nodes are unmarked on the way back, every simple path from the source to the destination is found.

key_points.point: Nodes on the current path are marked visited so the path never loops.
The path is printed when the destination is reached.
On backtracking the node is unmarked so other paths can use it.
key_points.quote: Visited[u]=0;
key_points.followup: What would go wrong without unmarking on backtrack?
key_points.followup_answer: A node used by one path could never appear in another, so some paths would be missed.

dsa.threaded_binary_search_tree.medium1.quality_note: points shortened; rthread now a point (repair 5)
dsa.threaded_binary_search_tree.medium1.reference_answer: In a right-in threaded binary tree, a node whose right pointer would be NULL instead points to its inorder successor; such a pointer is called a thread. The rthread field tells whether the right pointer is a thread or a real right child. In an inorder traversal, after visiting a node, if rthread is set you follow the thread straight to the successor; otherwise you go to the right child and then as far left as possible. So the traversal never needs to remember ancestors, and no explicit stack is needed.

key_points.point: An empty right pointer points to the node's inorder successor instead.

dsa.insertion_sort.hard2.quality_note: fine; relabelled medium (repair 4). Second point made specific to insertion sort: a selection-sort answer also matched it (repair 5)
dsa.insertion_sort.hard2.reference_answer: During insertion sort the sorted subarray at the start grows by one element in each iteration. The next element is inserted into its correct place in the sorted part by shifting every larger element one position to the right, so the sorted part stays sorted but its elements can still move later, unlike selection sort, where placed elements are final. This matters for performance because the work per element is the number of larger elements it must shift past: on a nearly sorted array almost nothing shifts, so insertion sort runs in close to linear time (best case n - 1 comparisons), while a reversed array gives the quadratic worst case.

key_points.point: Each new element is inserted by shifting larger elements in the sorted part one place right.
So it is fast on nearly sorted arrays, where few elements need shifting.

key_points.point: Creational patterns decide how and which objects get created, hiding the creation logic.
Structural patterns combine classes and objects into larger structures.
Behavioral patterns deal with how objects interact and communicate.

ooad.design_pattern_categories.hard2.reference_answer: The three categories group patterns by the kind of design problem they solve. Creational patterns decide how and which objects get created, hiding the creation logic from the code that uses the objects, for example making sure a class has only one instance. Structural patterns combine classes and objects into larger structures, the static structure of the design. Behavioral patterns deal with how objects interact and communicate at run time and how responsibilities are shared among them. This grouping makes us think about a design as three separate questions: how objects are created, how they are composed, and how they interact, which helps choose the right pattern for a problem.
